description: We are big data students that want to participate in this event to learn and improve our data engineering and AI skills and apply them to solve real world problems.
summary: A playable climate detective’s desk for MENA. Open a worn case folder, make a hypothesis, inspect real rainfall and satellite evidence, and build a conclusion you can defend.
details:
SaharaWatch is an interactive climate investigation tool built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” It helps people explore how rainfall has changed across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), where changes appear, how large they are, and how certain the evidence is.

Users can open one of six case files, follow a guided quiz, or investigate a question independently. They can select a country or map cell and time period, view rainfall maps and historical charts, compare locations, and examine satellite images. SaharaWatch calculates annual rainfall totals, trends, anomalies, confidence intervals and significance tests. Users can pin evidence, connect findings on a board, and export reports with sources and methodological details.

The project makes climate data and statistical reasoning easier to explore for students, educators, and the public. Its intended impact is to build evidence literacy: help users distinguish a single dry year from a longer-term trend, consider uncertainty, and understand the limits of what the data can establish. No learning outcomes have yet been measured.

SaharaWatch uses GPCP v2.3 monthly precipitation data distributed by NOAA’s Physical Sciences Laboratory, NASA GIBS Aqua and Terra MODIS imagery, and optional NASA POWER temperature observations. The app is built with Python and Streamlit, using Plotly, xarray, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, netCDF4 and Shapely. It runs in a web browser and needs no specialized hardware or paid AI service.

The project’s creative approach is a climate detective’s desk: users investigate case files, inspect clues, and build a conclusion they can defend. The team considered usability for people without programming or statistics experience, data provenance, missing observations, spatial resolution, uncertainty, and responsible interpretation. SaharaWatch supports historical exploration; it does not forecast drought, establish causes, or provide a complete drought-risk assessment.
